chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn Ishaq, from Sa'dan ibn Muslim, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Indeed, the believer supplicates to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, regarding his need, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Delay its answer, out of desire for his voice and his supplication.' So when it is the Day of Judgment, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'My servant, you supplicated to Me, so I delayed your answer, and your reward is such and such; and you supplicated to Me regarding such and such, so I delayed answering you, and your reward is such and such.'
He (peace be upon him) said: 'So the believer wishes that no supplication of his had been answered in the world, due to what he sees of the excellence of the reward.'
ai.seo_question: Why does Allah delay answering a believer's supplication?
ai.summary: In al-Kafi, Shaykh al-Kulayni records this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to illustrate the concept of 'Ikhtiyar' (divine choice) in supplication, where delay is not neglect but a means of accumulating greater reward. The Imam highlights that the believer's longing for Allah's response transforms the waiting period into an act of worship, resulting in such immense eschatological reward that the believer may prefer the delayed, high-value reward over immediate worldly fulfillment. This underscores the Shia scholarly view that patience in dua is a spiritual investment with exponential returns in the Hereafter.
